facts.statement: The genus Lycorhinus was described by Sidney H. Haughton in 1924.
facts.quote: authority: Haughton, 1924

facts.statement: Lycorhinus is known from the single species L. angustidens, originally described as a cynodont from a partial jaw found in the Upper Elliot Formation of South Africa.
facts.quote: It is known from a single species L. angustidens, that was named in 1924 by Sidney H. Haughton as a cynodont for a partial jaw found in the Upper Elliot Formation of South Africa.

facts.statement: The genus name Lycorhinus is derived from the Ancient Greek words for "wolf" and "nose".
facts.quote: The genus name is derived from the Ancient Greek words for "wolf" and "nose".

facts.statement: The original material of Lycorhinus has degraded to a single original tooth and an impression of the jaw, leading to multiple interpretations of its classification.
facts.quote: The limited material available, which has degraded over time to only be represented now by a single original tooth and the impression of the remaining jaw and teeth, has resulted in multiple different interpretations of the diagnostic nature and synonymy of Lycorhinus

facts.statement: A 1975 review accepted the synonymy of Lanasaurus scalpridens, named by Christopher Gow in 1975, with Lycorhinus angustidens.
facts.quote: The latest review of Lycorhinus accepted the synonymy of Lanasaurus scalpridens, named in 1975 by Christopher Gow for a maxilla from Golden Gate Highlands National Park, with Lycorhinus angustidens

facts.statement: Specimens of Lycorhinus were collected prior to 1914 by Dr. Martin Ricono from the Red Beds of Paballong in South Africa.
facts.quote: Prior to 1914, Dr. Martin Ricono collected multiple specimens from the "Red Beds" of Paballong, Mount Fletcher district of South Africa, sending them to the South African Museum.

facts.statement: Robert Broom incorrectly identified the type locality of Lycorhinus as Witkop near Burgersdorp in a 1932 review.
facts.quote: Robert Broom revisited Lycorhinus in a 1932 review of South African early mammals, incorrectly identifying the type locality as Witkop near Burgersdorp.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus was reidentified as a dinosaur in 1962 by Alfred Walter Crompton and Alan Jack Charig after being alerted by John Attridge.
facts.quote: The identity of Lycorhinus as a cynodont was maintained until 1962, when Alfred Walter Crompton and Alan Jack Charig described the new Triassic ornithischian Heterodontosaurus, and reidentified Lycorhinus as well after being alerted to it by John Attridge.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus lived during the Early Jurassic, specifically the Sinemurian stage.
facts.quote: Lycorhinus is a genus of heterodontosaurid ornithischian dinosaur that lived during the Early Jurassic, in the Sinemurian.

facts.statement: Uranium-lead dating in 2020 confirmed the Upper Elliot Formation spans from approximately 201.3 mya to at least 191.9 mya.
facts.quote: Uranium-lead dating done in 2020 confirmed that the Upper Elliot Formation spans approximately 10 million years of the Early Jurassic, from approximately the Triassic-Jurassic boundary 201.3 mya until at least the late Sinemurian 191.9 mya.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus is classified as a heterodontosaurid ornithischian dinosaur.
facts.quote: Lycorhinus is a genus of heterodontosaurid ornithischian dinosaur

facts.statement: Specimens from the Clarens Formation have been tentatively allied with Lycorhinus but may belong to indeterminate heterodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Tentative specimens from the Clarens Formation have also been considered allied with Lycorhinus, but they may be better treated as remains of indeterminate heterodontosaurids.

facts.statement: Charig and Crompton considered Lycorhinus a nomen dubium (dubious name) due to insufficient material to determine if it was the same genus as Heterodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Charig and Crompton found the limited and poor material of the latter was insufficient to determine if it could be the same genera and thus considered Lycorhinus a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Hopson argued that Lycorhinus is a valid diagnostic genus distinct from Heterodontosaurus and Abrictosaurus.
facts.quote: Hopson considered Lycorhinus diagnostic rather than dubious, and that at least three genera of heterodontosaurids were present.

facts.statement: Tentative specimens from the Clarens Formation have been considered allied with Lycorhinus.
facts.quote: Tentative specimens from the Clarens Formation have also been considered allied with Lycorhinus

facts.statement: Christopher Gow described a nearly complete maxilla found in the Red Beds at the "buck camp" of Golden Gate Highlands National Park.
facts.quote: Gow described a nearly complete maxilla he had found in the Red Beds at the "buck camp" of Golden Gate Highlands National Park, .

facts.statement: Christopher Gow described a new heterodontosaur maxilla found with James Kitching in 1984.
facts.quote: Gow described a new heterodontosaur maxilla he had found with James Kitching in 1984.

facts.statement: The maxilla specimen BP/1/5253 was found on the farm Bamboeskloof in Lady Grey, South Africa, less than 15 km from Heterodontosaurus localities and about 350 km south of the Lanasaurus type locality.
facts.quote: This maxilla, BP/1/5253, was found in the farm Bamboeskloof in Lady Grey, South Africa, at , less than 15 km from localities of Heterodontosaurus, approximately 130 km from the type locality of Lycorhinus, and about 350 km south of the type locality of Lanasaurus.

facts.statement: Two specimens considered possibly Lycorhinus were collected by Kermack and Mussett during a 1968 University of London expedition at the 6500 ft plateau of the Cave Sandstone (Clarens Formation).
facts.quote: Both were collected by Kermack and Mussett as part of the 1968 expedition of the University of London at the 6500 ft plateau of the Cave Sandstone (Clarens Formation) north of the eastern arm of Maboloka .

facts.statement: Paul Sereno redescribed specimen NHMUK RU A100 in 2012 to support referring Lanasaurus and other specimens to Lycorhinus.
facts.quote: Paul Sereno redescribed NHMUK RU A100 in 2012 to correct misidentifications of Thulborn and support a referral of Lanasaurus and all specimens to Lycorhinus.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus is a small herbivorous dinosaur about 1.2 meters in length that possessed long canines in its jaws.
facts.quote: Lycorhinus, including the remains described by Gow in 1975 as Lanasaurus, is a small (1.2 m in length) herbivorous dinosaur despite the long canines it sported in its jaws.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus consors was considered a nomen dubium because its description was inadequate.
facts.quote: L. consors was considered a nomen dubium due to its inadequate description.

facts.statement: In 1978, Thulborn maintained that Heterodontosaurus tucki and Abrictosaurus consors were species of Lycorhinus but proposed that Lanasaurus might not be a heterodontosaurid.
facts.quote: Thulborn maintained Heterodontosaurus tucki and Abrictosaurus consors as species of Lycorhinus in 1978, but supported the distinction of Lanasaurus and proposed it may not be a heterodontosaurid.

facts.statement: NHMUK RU A100 was referred to Lanasaurus, which was retained as a separate taxon from Lycorhinus due to a lack of overlapping anatomical material.
facts.quote: NHMUK RU A100 was instead referred to Lanasaurus, which was retained as a separate taxon due to the lack of overlap with Lycorhinus.

facts.statement: Crompton and Charig identified Lycorhinus as an ornithischian in 1962.
facts.quote: the ornithischian identity of Lycorhinus has been accepted since it was identified as such by Crompton and Charig in 1962

facts.statement: Romer classified Lycorhinus as a member of the ornithopod family Hypsilophodontidae.
facts.quote: Romer classified it as a member of the ornithopod family Hypsilophodontidae

facts.statement: Thulborn proposed in 1970 that Lycorhinus and Heterodontosaurus were synonyms.
facts.quote: The status of Lycorhinus as a relative of Heterodontosaurus was first put forward by Thulborn in 1970 when he established the two genera as synonyms

facts.statement: Sereno identified Lycorhinus as the earliest-diverging member of the Gondwanan clade Heterodontosaurinae.
facts.quote: Sereno found that key features of the teeth and jaws supported Lycorhinus as the earliest-diverging member of the Gondwanan clade Heterodontosaurinae

facts.statement: Baron and colleagues suggested in 2017 that ornithischians like Lycorhinus should be grouped with theropods in the clade Ornithoscelida.
facts.quote: In 2017, similarities between the skeletons of Heterodontosaurus and the early theropod Eoraptor were used by Matthew G. Baron and colleagues to suggest that ornithischians should be grouped with theropods in a group called Ornithoscelida

facts.statement: Dieudonné and colleagues hypothesized in 2020 that Lycorhinus was a basal marginocephalian rather than a distinct group.
facts.quote: In 2020, Paul-Emile Dieudonné and colleagues suggested that members of Heterodontosauridae were basal marginocephalians not forming their own natural group

facts.statement: A 2024 study by Fonseca and colleagues classified Lycorhinus as a derived heterodontosaurid sister to Abrictosaurus.
facts.quote: the 2024 study of André Fonseca and colleagues, who found Lycorhinus to be a more derived heterodontosaurid than previously recovered, as the sister to Abrictosaurus

facts.statement: Barrett suggested in 2000 that Lycorhinus was likely omnivorous based on its teeth and canine.
facts.quote: Paul Barrett suggested in 2000 that the premaxillary teeth and dentary canine were indications of heterodontosaurids being omnivorous

facts.statement: Butler and colleagues suggested in 2008 that Lycorhinus used its canines for defense and occasional omnivory.
facts.quote: Butler and colleagues suggested in 2008 that they were likely used for defense and occasional omnivory

facts.statement: Porro and colleagues suggested in 2010 that Lycorhinus ate tough, fibrous vegetation.
facts.quote: Porro and colleagues suggested in 2010 that the caniniforms were an indication of a diet of more tough, fibrous vegetation

facts.statement: Norman et al. suggested in 2011 that Lycorhinus did not use its canines for display or cropping vegetation.
facts.quote: Norman et al. suggested in 2011 alternatively that the canines were unlikely to have been used for display or cropping and rooting vegetation

facts.statement: Extensive tooth-to-tooth wear facets support the hypothesis that Lycorhinus was predominantly or exclusively herbivorous.
facts.quote: A predominantly or exclusively herbivorous diet in Lycorhinus could be directly supported by the extensive tooth-to-tooth wear facets it has

facts.statement: Fossils of Lycorhinus, consisting of loose teeth and a maxilla, were discovered in the Cape Province of the Upper Elliot Formation in South Africa.
facts.quote: Los restos fósiles del Lycorhinus, que consisten en consiste en dientes sueltos y un maxilar fueron descubiertos en la Provincia del Cabo, en la Formación Elliot Superior, Sudáfrica.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, SAM 3606, consists of a jaw found by Dr. M. Ricono.
facts.quote: El holotipo, SAM 3606 , consiste en una mandíbula encontrada por el Dr. M. Ricono.

facts.statement: Sidney H. Haughton named the genus Lycorhinus in 1924.
facts.quote: Sidney H. Haughton atribuyó a los restos en 1924

facts.statement: Alfred Walter Crompton recognized Lycorhinus as an ornithischian dinosaur in 1962.
facts.quote: Solo en 1962 Alfred Walter Crompton reconoció que era un dinosaurio ornitisquio.

facts.statement: The Upper Elliot Formation, where Lycorhinus was found, spans from the Hettangian to the Sinemurian stages, approximately 201.3 to 190.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: The Elliot Formation spans the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, with the lower Elliot being mid-Norian to Rhaetian, and the upper Elliot being Hettangian to Sinemurian; 201.3 to 190.8 million years ago.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus lived during the early Jurassic, approximately 203 to 197 million years ago, in what is now Africa.
facts.quote: que vivió a principios del período Jurásico inferior, hace aproximadamente 203 y 197 millones de años, en el Hettangiense y el Sinemuriense, en lo que hoy es África.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus lived in semi-desert environments and fed on vegetation.
facts.quote: Vagaba por los semidesiertos en busca de vegetales para comer

facts.statement: Lycorhinus usually walked on four legs but could run on its hind legs with its tail held upright when it perceived danger.
facts.quote: Solía caminar sobre cuatro patas, pero si percibía el peligro, podía correr sólo sobre las traseras manteniendo erguida su cola.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus used its beak to pull off shoots and chewed them using its wide, flat cheek teeth.
facts.quote: arrancaba los brotes con el pico, y los masticaba con los anchos y planos dientes de sus carrillos.

facts.statement: Two long, narrow canine-like teeth projected downward from the front of Lycorhinus's jaw.
facts.quote: En la parte anterior de la mandíbula sobresalían hacia abajo dos largos dientes estrechos similares a caninos.

facts.statement: Lycorhinus is classified in the family Heterodontosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Heterodontosauridae

facts.statement: Lycorhinus and Heterodontosaurus form the base of the family Heterodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Lycorhinus junto con Heterodontosaurus forman la base de la familia Heterodontosauridae.

facts.statement: Currently, only one species, Lycorhinus angustidens, is considered to exist within the genus Lycorhinus.
facts.quote: Actualmente se considera que solo posee una especie, Lycorhinus angustidens

facts.statement: Lanasaurus scalpridens was described by Christopher Gow in 1975 from the same horizon as Lycorhinus.
facts.quote: Lanasaurus scalpridens fue descrito por Christopher Gow en 1975 desde el mismo horizonte que Lycorhinus.

facts.statement: Christopher Gow concluded in 1990 that the holotype of Lanasaurus scalpridens was actually a specimen of Lycorhinus angustidens, a view commonly accepted since then.
facts.quote: El mismo Gow en 1990 concluyó que el holotipo de Lanasaurus era en realidad un espécimen de Lycorhinus angustidens.

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database lists Abrictosaurus consors as the type species for the genus Lycorhinus.
facts.quote: Type species: Abrictosaurus consors
